planting.note: Root softwood tip cuttings in late spring, or divide established mats, into a gritty, fast-draining scree mix; shear lightly after bloom to keep the mound dense.

directions: Forming a tight, long-blooming mound of white-to-blue-violet flowers in subalpine meadow and ponderosa-pine-opening habitat, this phlox offers true-blue tones distinct from the pink and magenta of eastern creeping phlox already in cultivation. Established plants resent wet feet far more than drought, so resist the urge to baby it with summer water. In hot lowland gardens below its native zone it struggles more with humidity than cold.

planting.note: Root 3-4 inch softwood tip cuttings in late spring into lean, rocky, basalt-derived soil on a slope or raised bed; avoid compost or overhead irrigation once established.

directions: A dense, slightly woody, needle-leaved cushion native to Columbia Plateau and Rocky Mountain ponderosa pine openings, this phlox fills the same ecological niche in the garden as imported creeping phlox cultivars but from drier, more easterly sites, giving Intermountain West gardeners an authentic regional alternative. This species wants lean, rocky, basalt-derived soil — amending with compost or rich garden loam causes rot and rank, short-lived growth.

planting.note: Root cuttings of non-flowering shoots in early summer in a sandy mix, or sow stratified seed, into thin rocky soil over a gravel-heavy raised bed mimicking shallow basalt scabland.

directions: A Columbia Plateau scabland endemic forming tight cushions in purple, pink, and magenta-red, this is the true straight species — most Phlox douglasii sold in commerce is actually a Phlox subulata hybrid group, making this a genuine gap worth distinguishing clearly. It tolerates more part-shade than most western cushion phlox but still needs excellent drainage; a top-dressing of pea gravel around the crown reduces rot risk through wet winters.

planting.note: Direct-sow with cold stratification where it will stay, or use deep plug trays, since the deep taproot makes transplanting difficult; into lean, stony, sparsely vegetated ground.

directions: A true shortgrass-prairie taprooted mat phlox blooming white to pale pink and purple in May, this species fills a prairie-rock-garden and xeric-trough niche that the dataset's largely woodland or eastern Phlox species don't cover. It thrives in lean, stony, sparsely vegetated ground and will rot or be crowded out in rich, well-watered perennial beds — pair it with other shortgrass prairie species rather than mesic companions.

planting.note: Divide mat-forming clumps in early spring into consistently moist to seasonally saturated, alkaline soil; add a little lime if local water is naturally acidic.

directions: Botanically unusual for the genus, this is a wetland and fen phlox from alkaline wet meadows and geothermal-area margins rather than the dry scree most Phlox occupy, useful for gardeners wanting a true-species Phlox for a bog garden, pond margin, or seasonally wet alkaline soil. Flowers range from white to lilac, lavender, or pink, often with a bluish sheen, over an unusually long May-July bloom window. A streamside bench or fen edge suits it far better than a dry scree bed.

planting.note: Divide cushion offsets in spring into a mineral, humus-free scree or tufa mix raised for drainage, with crushed dolomite or limestone chips to mimic native substrate.

directions: A true high-alpine cushion species from the southern Rockies at 6,100 to 14,000 feet, this phlox forms a dense, fragrant, nearly stemless evergreen mat prized in rock-garden-society circles for its scent as much as its flowers. It does not tolerate hot, humid summers or wet winter crowns, so give it the coldest, most open site available. Treat any bloom in the first two years as a bonus, not an expectation, since growth is very slow regardless of propagation method.

planting.note: Direct-sow with light cold stratification into a pinyon-juniper-style xeric bed with sharp drainage; also amenable to basal cuttings in spring.

directions: An upright, not mat-forming, desert and pinyon-juniper phlox from the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau, this species carries larger, longer-tubed pink-to-white flowers than the cushion species, a good choice for xeric gardens wanting phlox form and color without a creeping habit. It needs sharp drainage and minimal summer water once established but tolerates more heat than alpine and subalpine phlox species, a good bridge plant between true alpine phlox and lowland xeriscape design.

planting.note: Divide mat offsets in spring into full sun with sharp scree drainage; performs poorly in humid, low-elevation gardens without excellent air circulation and winter drainage.

directions: An Olympic Mountains and east-Cascades alpine endemic forming a dense, hairy-glandular mat with distinctive leaves in groups of three and solitary white, stemless flowers, this phlox blooms later, in July and August, than most other western rock-garden phlox, extending the bloom season into midsummer. It is adapted to rocky, open, high-elevation sites and should be treated as a specialist alpine-trough subject rather than a general border plant.
